title: Wavefront Arbiter: kernel-aware wave-slice scheduler and kernel-pricing model for balanced fairness/latency
creator: Marco Alvarez
description:
Summary:
We need a new scheduler prototype (Wavefront Arbiter) that treats prefill+decode as a sequence of small "wave-slices" and applies a kernel-aware pricing model to balance latency-critical requests against throughput-oriented batches. Instead of binary phase-splitting heuristics, Wavefront uses short-lived micro-slices, kernel cost hints (fast dense GEMM vs attention-sparse kernels), and tenant credit adjustments to make deterministic trade-offs between 95th-p95 latency and sustained throughput.

Background:
Current prefill/decode arbitration suffers from oscillation between latency-focused hedging and throughput-driven consolidation. Existing approaches either prioritize low-latency at high cost or maximize GPU utilization at the expense of tail latency for high-priority tenants. Many tickets have explored phase splitting and kernel hints; this ticket is a pragmatic, end-to-end scheduler+pricing experiment that operationalizes kernel selection signals into scheduling decisions.

Goals:
- Reduce 95th percentile latency for priority-tenants by 20-30% under mixed workloads, without dropping baseline throughput by more than 8%.
- Provide an instrumentation surface that exposes per-kernel cost breakdowns used by the arbiter so we can audit decisions.
- Produce a rollout plan to validate on Dedicated pools and then the hosted fleet.

Design overview (high level):
1) Wave-slice unit: split requests into micro slices (configurable token-window, default 8 tokens) so scheduling decisions are more granular than whole-prefill or whole-decode phases.
2) Kernel pricing model: each kernel variant (dense, sparse-attn, quantized-4bit) publishes an estimated cost vector: {gpu_ms, memory_pressure, expected-kv-size}. The arbiter translates that into a normalized price per-token for scheduling comparisons.
3) Credit-based fairer queues: tenants have soft credits (SLAs) used to discount price for latency-sensitive workloads; credits replenish based on historical usage.
4) Hedged fast-path: if a high-priority slice is delayed beyond a micro timeout, spawn an opportunistic hedged decode on a cheaper kernel with degraded quality but bounded latency.
5) Kernel hint feedback: runtime probes can test a kernel on a short sample to validate price assumptions; those probes feed back into the price model.

API/Config changes:
- route config gets new fields: wave_slice_size, kernel_price_profile, latency_credit_policy, hedged_timeout_ms.
- console exposes per-route price breakdown and historical decisions.

Implementation plan:
- Week 1: RFC + simulation harness (single-host simulator) that replays production traces and allows plugging kernel price tables.
- Week 2: implement arbiter + micro-slicing in serving runtime; wire kernel price signals from the kernel selector.
- Week 3: integration test + benchmark on dev Dedicated pool; collect p50/p95/p99 and throughput metrics.
- Week 4: Canary on <10% traffic in hosted API for two non-critical routes.

Metrics and success criteria (initial targets):
- Priority tenant p95 latency: -25% vs baseline on mixed read/write trace.
- Overall token throughput: >= 92% of baseline sustained throughput.
- Kernel utilization variance reduced by at least 15% (fewer extreme peaks).
- Decision explainability: per-request decision logs present in Console for >95% of sampled slices.

Acceptance criteria (see field):

Notes on fairness and safety:
- Credits are soft: default is to prioritize isolation for P0 customers but avoid starvation for long-tailed tenants.
- Hedged fast-path must be limited to kernel variants that respect model correctness constraints (fallback to less-accurate kernels only when explicitly allowed by route config).

Links and artifacts:
- RFC (internal doc): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Wavefront+Arbiter+RFC
- Simulator repo (branch): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime-sim/pull/127
- Kernel hints spec: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KERNEL-HINTS-EXAMPLE
- Early benchmark ticket: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/issues/54

Operational concerns and rollout:
- Start in Dedicated staging pools where we control tenant mix.
- Enable verbose sampling and a throttled decision-logging pipeline to avoid telemetry storms.
- Backout plan: if p95 increases for any critical customer by >15% during canary, auto-disable Wavefront for that pool and revert to baseline arbiter.

Risks:
- Price model drift if kernel costs change between probes and scheduled execution; mitigate by short probe windows and conservative safety margins.
- Complexity of micro-slices increasing scheduling overhead; measure overhead per-request and cap micro-slicing for very short requests.
- Interactions with autoscaling: micro-slicing could increase temporary resource fragmentation; test with autoscaler on in simulator.

Progress updates:
- 2026-01-21: RFC posted and initial feedback from Evan Li and Ruth Chen. Decision: include hedged fast-path but gate it.
- 2026-02-02: Simulator ingest pipeline implemented; replayed one week of trace (mixed park/startup workloads). Initial sim shows 18% p95 improvement for priority tenants but 10% throughput drop.
- 2026-02-16: Kernel price model MVP added to runtime; price table supports dense/quantized/sparse kernels.
- 2026-02-28: Micro-slice implementation landed behind feature flag (PR #1234). Integration tests show ~1.8% CPU overhead on scheduler thread at 8-token slice size.
- 2026-03-03: Canary plan drafted and QA checklist completed.
- 2026-03-10: Dev Dedicated run for 48 hours: p95 -22% for priority group, throughput -6.2%, kernel utilization variance -18%. Observed two edge cases where tiny requests (<=6 tokens) experienced spurious hedging; plan to exclude requests shorter than slice size.

- Gradual rollout to Dedicated fleets: 2026-03-23 to 2026-04-06
- Hosted API experiment: 2026-04-10 onwards (after Dedicated stability window).
